analysis.one_liner: Requires the largest banks' credit cards to work on competing payment networks so merchants can avoid costly routing.
analysis.headline: The bill drew 9 cosponsors split between both parties but never received a committee vote, dying in the House Financial Services Committee when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required banks with more than $100 billion in assets to issue credit cards that can be processed on at least two payment networks, with at least one coming from outside the two largest networks (Visa and Mastercard). That would let stores route transactions over cheaper networks instead of being locked into the dominant ones. It also banned penalties for routing choices and directed the Federal Reserve to publish a list of payment networks deemed national security risks. It never received a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Merchants who accept credit cards — from big retail chains to small businesses — would gain the right to route transactions over competing networks and negotiate lower swipe fees instead of accepting the network terms banks set. Consumers would benefit indirectly if merchants pass fee savings into lower prices, as supporters argue typically happens in competitive markets; whether that pass-through is full or fast is the central open question. Community banks, credit unions, and closed-loop systems like American Express were carved out entirely.

how_it_helps.text: Requires covered issuers — banks with more than $100 billion in assets — to make each credit card usable on at least two payment networks, at least one of which cannot be among the two largest by cards issued, breaking the Visa/Mastercard routing lock-in for merchants.
Prohibits issuers and networks from penalizing merchants for routing a transaction over a cheaper network, or from imposing volume requirements that force transactions onto a particular network.

Bars exclusive arrangements and proprietary security or tokenization technology that other networks cannot use to process the same transaction, so merchants and rival networks can actually compete on processing.

Directs the Federal Reserve, consulting Treasury, to publish and update a public list of payment card networks that pose a national security risk or are owned, operated, or sponsored by a foreign state entity.

analysis.who_pays: Visa and Mastercard, whose near-duopoly over credit card routing would lose exclusive processing volume, and the largest card-issuing banks, which collect interchange (swipe) fees on every transaction and fund rewards programs out of that revenue. If competition compresses those fees, rewards could shrink or other card costs could rise; consumers who rely heavily on rewards would bear part of that. Small issuers under $100 billion and closed-loop networks like American Express pay nothing — the bill exempts them.
analysis.who_pays_short: Visa, Mastercard, and the biggest card-issuing banks

drawbacks.text: The savings go to merchants first, and whether shoppers actually see them is unproven: after Congress imposed a similar routing rule on debit cards in 2010, merchant savings were not consistently passed through to consumers (some retailers simply kept the difference), so the consumer benefit here is indirect and uncertain.

Banks and card networks argued that compressing interchange revenue would force cuts to credit card rewards and could shift costs to cardholders — the fees the bill targets are what fund points, miles, and cash-back programs.

The bill leaves most of the market structurally untouched: it applies only to issuers with over $100 billion in assets and exempts three-party systems where the issuer owns the network, so American Express and Discover's closed-loop models and the entire community bank and credit union sector keep the existing arrangement.

Enforcement is narrowed as well as expanded: the bill strips the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau of any authority to enforce the new requirements, leaving the Federal Reserve as the sole enforcer.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: This is a genuine pro-competition measure aimed at a two-network routing duopoly, and merchants' negotiating leverage would increase immediately. But the consumer case rests on an assumption — that merchants pass swipe-fee savings into prices — that the debit-card precedent only partly supports, and the rewards tradeoff is real for households that rely on points and cash back. The carve-outs for small issuers and closed-loop networks make it a targeted strike at Visa, Mastercard, and the largest banks rather than a rewrite of the payment system. On balance the public likely gains modestly and indirectly, while the concentrated interests on both sides — retailers versus banks and networks — fight over a very large fee pool.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the House Financial Services Committee in June 2023, and the committee never took it up — no hearing, no markup, no vote — so it simply expired when the Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Rep. Lance Gooden introduced the Credit Card Competition Act of 2023 on June 7, 2023, with Reps. Zoe Lofgren, Tom Tiffany, and Jeff Van Drew as original cosponsors.
The same day, the bill was referred to the House Committee on Financial Services, the committee with jurisdiction over banking and payments.

That referral was the last action ever taken: the bill accumulated 9 cosponsors (5 Democrats, 4 Republicans) but the committee never scheduled it for consideration, and it died at the end of the 118th Congress in January 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Visa, Mastercard, and the largest card-issuing banks are better off: the routing lock-in and swipe-fee structure the bill targeted stay fully intact. Merchants gained nothing, and the card networks face no new competition from the federal government — though a Senate companion version kept the idea alive in public debate.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Visa, Mastercard, and big card-issuing banks

sides.party_line_note: Support was bipartisan from the start — the lead sponsor was a Republican joined by a Democratic original cosponsor, and the 9 cosponsors split 5 Democrats to 4 Republicans — but the bill never reached a floor vote, so member-level opposition was never formally recorded.

industries.note: The bill strikes directly at their routing duopoly: every large-issuer credit card would have to work on at least one network outside the two largest, and merchants could no longer be penalized for routing elsewhere. Their interest in preserving exclusive routing runs against merchants' costs, which flow into consumer prices.

industries.industry: Large card-issuing banks (over $100 billion in assets)
industries.note: These banks collect interchange fees on every credit transaction and fund rewards from that revenue; routing competition would compress the fees. Only banks above the $100 billion threshold are covered, so the cost is concentrated on the biggest issuers.

Stores of all sizes would get routing choice and negotiating leverage over swipe fees. Their savings reach ordinary people only to the extent merchants pass them into prices, which is the bill's key uncertainty.
The bill exempts three-party systems where the issuer owns the network, locking American Express and Discover's closed-loop models out of the new requirements while their larger rivals face them.

They keep their current interchange arrangements because issuers under $100 billion are exempt, but trade groups argued in public debate that the exemption would not protect them from downward pressure on rates across the market.
